analogy.p: Think of a network as roads. A **LAN** is like the roads on a single housing estate: short, owned by the local council, quick to travel and easy to control. A **WAN** is like the national motorway network joining many towns: it covers huge distances, is owned and maintained by a big authority (like the telecoms companies) and you pay to use it. **Bandwidth** is the number of lanes: more lanes allow more cars (data) per minute. The **number of devices** is the number of cars on the road: lots of cars at rush hour causes a traffic jam. The **transmission media** is the road surface (a smooth fibre motorway versus a bumpy country lane of Wi-Fi), and the **error rate** is the number of cars that break down and have to go back and start again. The analogy breaks down because data is split into packets that can each take different routes and be re-sent, whereas a car makes one journey.

bullets: Define a **network** as two or more computing devices connected so that they can share data and resources.
Describe a **LAN** and a **WAN**, including area covered, ownership of the infrastructure and typical examples.
Explain why networks are built: sharing files, printers, internet connections and software, and central management.
Explain the factors that affect **performance**: bandwidth, number of devices, transmission media, error rate and others.
Apply the ideas to a scenario, for example why a school network is slow at lunchtime, and suggest sensible improvements.
Carry out simple calculations such as file download time = file size divided by bandwidth, with correct units.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.3 (Networks, connections and protocols) begins with the **types of network** and the **factors that affect network performance**. You must be able to define a **LAN (Local Area Network)** and a **WAN (Wide Area Network)**, give examples of each, and explain how they differ in size, ownership and speed. You must also be able to describe the factors that make a network faster or slower, such as bandwidth, the number of connected devices, the transmission media used and the error rate, and to apply them to a given scenario. This is assessed on Paper 1 (Computer systems) as short definition questions (1 to 2 marks), compare questions (3 to 4 marks) and scenario-based discussion questions (6 marks).

bullets: **Sharing files**: one copy of a document is stored centrally and many users can open it, which avoids duplicated or out-of-date copies.
**Sharing hardware**: printers, scanners and storage are shared, reducing cost because the organisation buys fewer devices.
**Sharing an internet connection**: one connection to the ISP can serve every device through a router.
**Central management**: an administrator can install updates, set permissions and back up everything from one place.
**Communication**: email, messaging and video calls are possible between users on the network.

**Disadvantages**: networks cost money to set up and maintain, are a **security risk** because unauthorised users or malware can spread between devices, and if the network fails users may lose access to shared resources.
core.h: What is a network and why do we build them?
core.p: A **network** is a collection of computers and other devices, such as printers, phones and servers, that are connected together so that they can **communicate and share resources**. The connection can use cables (copper or fibre optic) or wireless signals (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data). Networks are built because sharing is far more efficient than every device working alone. A school with 500 computers could not afford a printer, a copy of every file and an internet connection for each one, so these are shared across the network and managed centrally.

bullets: Definition to learn: a LAN covers a **small geographical area** on a **single site**.

The organisation **owns the infrastructure** (switches, cables, access points) and does not rent it from a telecoms company, so it has full control and does not pay ongoing line charges for the internal network.
Typically uses **Ethernet** cables (copper or fibre) and/or **Wi-Fi**; devices are connected through a **switch** or wireless access point.
Examples: a home network, a school or office network, a computer lab, a games room at a café.
**Advantages**: fast speeds because distances are short, easy and cheap to expand a little, simple to manage and secure because it is all on one site under one owner.
**Limitation**: it cannot connect places that are far apart; for that a WAN is needed.
core.p: A **LAN** is a network that covers a **small geographical area**, usually a single site such as one building, one school, one office or a home. Almost all of the hardware that makes up a LAN, such as cabling, switches and wireless access points, is **owned and managed by the organisation that uses it**. Because distances are short, a LAN can use fast, high-quality connections and so offers **high data transfer speeds** and low delay. Your home Wi-Fi network is a LAN, and so is the network that connects the computers in a school computer room.

bullets: Definition to learn: a WAN covers a **large geographical area** and connects LANs.
Infrastructure is usually **owned by telecoms companies** and **leased** by organisations, so there are ongoing costs.
Uses routers, leased lines, fibre-optic cables, satellite and mobile networks to join sites across long distances.
Examples: the **Internet**, a bank linking its branches nationally, a multinational company linking offices in London, Paris and Tokyo, a mobile phone network.
Data usually travels at **slower speeds** and with **more delay and errors** than inside a LAN because the distance is much greater and the data passes through many routers.
A WAN is **more expensive to set up and maintain** than a LAN and is harder to secure because data travels over third-party links.
core.p: A **WAN** is a network that covers a **large geographical area**, such as a town, a country or even the whole world. It is used to connect **LANs together**, for example the head office and branch offices of a bank in different cities. The key difference from a LAN is that no single organisation can lay its own cables across a country, so a WAN normally uses infrastructure **owned by telecommunications companies** (telephone lines, fibre cables, undersea cables and satellites) which are **leased or rented**. The **Internet** is the best-known example: it is a worldwide network of networks, so it is a WAN.

bullets: **Area**: LAN covers a small area on one site, whereas a WAN covers a large area such as a country or the world.
**Ownership**: the organisation owns the LAN hardware and cabling, whereas WAN infrastructure is generally owned by telecoms companies and leased.
**Speed**: LANs usually have higher data transfer speeds, whereas WAN links are generally slower per connection because of distance and shared lines.
**Cost**: a LAN is cheaper to build and run; a WAN is more expensive because of leasing fees and long-distance equipment.
**Example**: school network (LAN) versus the Internet (WAN).
**Connection between them**: a WAN is often made by joining several LANs together through routers.
core.p: In an exam you are often asked to compare the two, and the marks come from pairing a point about a LAN with the matching point about a WAN. The most reliable comparison points are **area covered**, **who owns the infrastructure**, **speed**, **cost** and **examples**. Always make the comparison explicit (using words such as 'whereas' or 'but') rather than just listing two separate descriptions, because a mark scheme usually awards one mark per comparative pair.

bullets: Bandwidth is measured in **bits per second**: 1 kbit/s = 1000 bit/s, 1 Mbit/s = 1000 kbit/s, 1 Gbit/s = 1000 Mbit/s.
**Higher bandwidth = faster transfer** and the ability to support more users and more demanding applications at once.
A school may have a 1 Gbit/s link to the Internet because hundreds of users share it; a home might have 50 to 100 Mbit/s.
**Remember the units**: network speeds use **bits** but file sizes use **bytes**. 1 byte = 8 bits, so a 100 MB file is 800 Mbit.
Download time (seconds) = **file size in bits divided by bandwidth in bits per second**.
Do not confuse bandwidth with the **latency** (delay before data starts to arrive); latency is not named in the J277 specification but is worth understanding as a different idea.
core.p: **Bandwidth** is the **amount of data that can be transmitted across a network connection in a given time**, usually measured in **bits per second** (for example Mbit/s or Gbit/s). It is the capacity of the link, a bit like the width of a pipe: a wider pipe lets more water through each second. A higher bandwidth means files download faster and more data can be sent at the same time, which is particularly important for video streaming, online gaming and video calls. Bandwidth is the maximum, and the speed you actually achieve is often lower because the capacity is shared and affected by errors.

bullets: If a 100 Mbit/s link is shared equally by 10 users, each gets about **10 Mbit/s**; with 20 users, about **5 Mbit/s** (the graph in this note shows this).
More devices also means more **collisions or waiting** on a shared connection, and more load on the **switch, router and server**.
It is the number of devices **actively using** the network at the same time that matters most, not simply the number connected.
Heavy users matter: one device downloading a huge file or streaming 4K video can use a large share of the bandwidth and slow others.
**Peak times** (evenings at home, break times at school) are when performance usually drops.
Solution: **increase bandwidth**, add more switches or access points, or limit demanding activities (for example quality of service rules).
core.h: Performance factor 2: number of devices (users) connected
core.p: Bandwidth is **shared** between every device using a connection. When only one device is using the link it can use all of the bandwidth, but as more devices connect and use the network at the same time, each gets a smaller share. This is why a school network feels fast during a lesson with one class online but slow at lunchtime when hundreds of students stream video at once. Too much demand on a link causes **congestion**, in the same way too many cars on a road cause a traffic jam, and data has to wait its turn.

bullets: **Copper cable (Ethernet)**: electrical signals; cheap and common; speeds often up to 1 Gbit/s or more on newer cable; signal weakens over distance (usually about 100 m for a single run).
**Fibre optic cable**: pulses of **light**; **much higher bandwidth**, can run for much longer distances, and is **not affected by electrical interference**; more expensive to install.

**Wireless (Wi-Fi)**: radio waves; convenient and no cables, but **slower and less reliable**, can suffer **interference** from other networks or devices, and the signal weakens through walls and with distance.
Wireless is also **less secure** than wired by default because anyone in range can attempt to connect, so it needs encryption and passwords.
Choosing media is a **trade-off**: fibre for the backbone and long links, copper Ethernet for connecting desktops, Wi-Fi for laptops, tablets and phones.
For a 6 mark answer, link the medium to the **scenario**: for a server room use wired connections for reliability; for visitors use Wi-Fi for convenience.
core.p: **Transmission media** are the physical or wireless paths that carry the data between devices. The type chosen strongly affects the **speed, reliability and range** of a connection. **Wired** connections (copper Ethernet cables or fibre optic cables) generally give a faster and more reliable connection than **wireless**, because the signal is contained in a cable and is less affected by interference. Wireless (Wi-Fi) is convenient and allows movement, but the signal weakens with distance and walls and can be disrupted by interference, and the airwaves are shared among all the devices.

bullets: Causes of errors: **interference** (electrical equipment, other Wi-Fi networks), **weak signal** over long distance or through walls, damaged or poor-quality cables, and congested equipment dropping packets.
Wireless connections and long WAN links generally have **higher error rates** than short wired LAN connections; fibre optic has very low error rates.
Retransmission **uses extra bandwidth and time**, so downloads and video calls become slow, buffer or freeze.
Reduce errors by using **better quality cables (shielded copper or fibre)**, moving devices closer to the access point, reducing interference and keeping equipment in good condition.
This links to the idea that data is split into packets with a **header** containing checks; see the later topic on packet switching.
In an answer say 'packets have to be **resent**, which **slows the network**' rather than just 'errors make it slow'.
core.p: Data is sent across a network in small units called **packets**. Sometimes a packet is **corrupted** (the data changes in transit because of interference or a weak signal) or lost. The receiving device detects this using error checking (such as a checksum) and asks for the packet to be **sent again**. This is called **retransmission**. The **error rate** is how often this happens. A high error rate means many packets have to be resent, which wastes bandwidth and increases the time taken, so the **effective speed falls even though the bandwidth has not changed**.

bullets: **Network topology**: in a star network a failed cable only affects one device but all traffic passes through the central switch; in a mesh network there are many paths so traffic can be shared and rerouted.
**Hardware quality**: old routers and switches limit speeds; the slowest device in the path sets the limit (a bottleneck).
**Server specification**: a server with a slow processor, little RAM or slow storage cannot respond to many requests quickly.
**Distance**: the further the signal travels, the weaker it becomes and the more errors and delay appear, particularly for wireless.
**Background traffic and malware**: unwanted programs or updates running in the background use bandwidth.
**Time of day**: peak usage reduces the share each device gets.
core.p: Beyond the four main factors, many other things influence how well a network performs. Examiners award marks for sensible, well-explained extra points, particularly in the scenario-based 6 mark question. The **layout (topology)** of the network, the **quality and speed of the hardware** (switches, routers and servers) and the **distance** between devices all matter. A server that is too slow or has too little memory will become a **bottleneck**, because every request has to wait for it, even if the network cables are fast.

bullets: Formula: **time (s) = file size (bits) ÷ bandwidth (bits per s)**; rearranged: bandwidth = size ÷ time; size = bandwidth × time.
Convert: **MB × 8 = Mbit** (1 byte = 8 bits), and 1 Mbit = 1 000 000 bits.
Example: 750 MB file on a 100 Mbit/s link: 750 × 8 = 6000 Mbit; 6000 ÷ 100 = **60 seconds**.
Example with sharing: the same link shared equally by 25 users gives 100 ÷ 25 = 4 Mbit/s each, so 6000 ÷ 4 = **1500 s = 25 minutes**.
Convert seconds to minutes by dividing by 60 and state the unit of your answer.
This is an ideal figure; real transfer is slower because of **errors, retransmission and other traffic**.
core.p: A common numerical question asks how long a file takes to transfer. The key is to make the **units match**. Bandwidth is given in **bits per second**, while file sizes are usually in **bytes**, so convert the file size to bits first by multiplying bytes by 8. Then use **time = file size (bits) divided by bandwidth (bits per second)**. If the bandwidth is shared, divide it by the number of users first. Always show the conversion step because mark schemes give a mark for it.

bullets: **Increase bandwidth**: pay for a faster internet connection or upgrade to fibre, so more data can be sent per second for all users.
**Use wired connections** (Ethernet or fibre) for important or busy devices, so there is less interference and a lower error rate.
**Add more switches or wireless access points** so the load is spread and fewer devices share each one.
**Upgrade old hardware** such as routers, switches and servers that act as a bottleneck.
**Limit or schedule heavy use** (for example block streaming sites at school, schedule backups for night time).
**Improve layout or topology**, for example a mesh to provide alternative routes, at higher cost.
core.h: Improving the performance of a network
core.p: Because the factors above can be controlled, a network manager can usually improve a slow network, and in a 6 mark question you should link each improvement to the problem it solves. Suggestions should be realistic for the scenario (a school, an office, a home) and you should explain **why** they help, not just name them. Remember that every improvement also has a cost, and the best answers mention the trade-off.

bullets: **Client-server and peer-to-peer** (next point): how devices on a LAN or WAN are organised.
**Network hardware**: NICs, switches, routers and wireless access points are what actually build a LAN; a router joins a LAN to a WAN.
**Topologies**: star and mesh layouts affect performance and reliability.
**Units of data (section 1.2)**: bits, bytes, MB and Gbit are needed for bandwidth calculations.
**Network security (section 1.4)**: sharing connections increases risk, so firewalls and encryption matter.
**Cloud computing**: relies on a fast, reliable WAN connection to remote servers.
core.p: This topic is the foundation for the rest of section 1.3. Understanding what a LAN and WAN are makes it easier to understand **why** hardware such as switches and routers exists, how the **Internet** connects many networks, and why **client-server** and **peer-to-peer** models exist. Bandwidth links to file sizes and units from section 1.2, error checking links to packets and protocols, and the security issues of sharing connect to section 1.4 (network security).

exam: **Command words**: 'Describe' = give features; 'Explain' = give a reason and link it using because or so; 'Compare' = similarities or differences, each point about both; 'Discuss' (6 marks) = balanced points, a conclusion.
**1 mark definitions**: LAN = 'a network covering a small geographical area (such as one building or site)'; WAN = 'a network covering a large geographical area'. Add the word **geographical**.
**2 mark questions** usually need a point and a development, for example 'bandwidth is shared (1) so each device gets a smaller share and is slower (1)'.
**3 to 4 mark compare questions**: pair up area, ownership/infrastructure, speed and cost. Use 'whereas'. Add one example of each (school network, Internet).

**6 mark scenario questions** (for example a slow school network): choose 3 to 4 relevant factors, explain each in the context of the scenario, suggest an improvement and give a short conclusion. Use level-of-response structure: point, reason, link to scenario.
**Calculations**: show the conversion (bytes to bits), the formula and the unit. Marks are usually given for the conversion and the division even if the final answer is wrong.
Name the **specific** transmission medium (fibre optic, copper, Wi-Fi) and give a reason (light pulses, no interference, higher bandwidth) rather than just 'better cable'.
Use the phrase '**packets have to be resent**' for error rate and '**bandwidth is shared**' for number of devices; these are model phrases.
Avoid vague words like 'faster' alone; say 'more data can be transmitted per second'.
Always relate the answer to the scenario given (school, hospital, bank) to reach the top levels of a 6 mark answer.

mistakes.r: Say **area covered**: a LAN covers a small geographical area such as one site, a WAN covers a large geographical area. Mention **ownership** (organisation versus telecoms company) for the extra mark.
mistakes.w: A LAN is just a small network and a WAN is a big one.

mistakes.r: The Internet is a **WAN** (a worldwide network of networks) but it is **not the only one**; a company linking its offices is also a WAN.
mistakes.w: The Internet is a LAN / the Internet is the only WAN.

mistakes.r: Bandwidth is the **amount of data that can be transmitted in a given time** (bits per second). Speed also depends on other factors such as errors and the number of users.
mistakes.w: Bandwidth is how fast the network is.

mistakes.r: The **bandwidth is shared** between all devices using the connection, so each device gets a smaller share.
mistakes.w: More devices make the network slow because they are heavy / the wires get full.

mistakes.r: Packets that are corrupted must be **resent (retransmitted)**, which wastes bandwidth and time.
Wired connections are usually **faster and more reliable**; Wi-Fi is more convenient but suffers from interference and weaker signals.
mistakes.w: Wi-Fi is faster because there are no wires.

mistakes.r: A byte is **8 bits**: convert MB to Mbit by multiplying by 8 before dividing by the bandwidth in Mbit/s.
mistakes.w: Using MB and Mbit as the same unit in a calculation.

mistakes.r: Make each point a **comparison** using 'whereas' or 'but' so every pair earns a mark.
mistakes.w: Listing the LAN and WAN descriptions separately in a compare question.

summary: You need to define a LAN (small area, one site, owned by the organisation) and a WAN (large area, leased infrastructure, e.g. the Internet), compare them, and explain how bandwidth, number of devices, transmission media and error rate affect network performance. It matters because every later networking topic, and 6 mark scenario questions on Paper 1, build on these ideas.

terms.d: Two or more computing devices connected together so that they can communicate and share data and resources.
A network covering a small geographical area, usually a single site, with the infrastructure owned by the organisation that uses it.
A network covering a large geographical area that connects LANs together, usually using infrastructure leased from telecommunications companies.
A worldwide network of networks; the best-known example of a WAN.
The amount of data that can be transmitted across a connection in a given time, measured in bits per second.
The smallest unit of data, a single 0 or 1; there are 8 bits in a byte.
A small unit of data sent across a network, containing a header and the data being sent.
The physical (cable) or wireless paths used to carry data between devices, such as copper, fibre optic and Wi-Fi.
How often data is corrupted or lost during transmission; errors cause packets to be resent.
Sending a packet again because it was corrupted or lost the first time.
Too much data trying to use a network connection at once, so data has to wait and performance falls.
The slowest part of a system, which limits the performance of the whole path (for example an old switch or slow server).
Unwanted signals, such as from other devices or networks, that disrupt a transmission, especially wireless.
A cable that carries data as pulses of light; very high bandwidth, long range and little interference.
The delay between sending a request and receiving the response (not named in the specification, but useful to understand).
A dedicated communications link rented from a telecoms provider, often used to build a WAN.

worked.ans: A LAN covers a small geographical area such as a single building, whereas a WAN covers a large geographical area such as a country or the world. The organisation that uses the LAN owns the cabling and equipment, whereas a WAN normally uses infrastructure owned by telecoms companies that is leased. A LAN generally has higher data transfer speeds and is cheaper to set up, whereas a WAN has lower speeds and higher costs. For example, a school computer room is a LAN but the Internet is a WAN.

Pair one point about speed or cost.

worked.ans: At lunchtime many students connect and stream video, so the bandwidth of the school's connection is shared between many devices and each gets a smaller share, which makes pages load slowly. If the connection has a low bandwidth it will be used up quickly, so the school could pay for a higher bandwidth or fibre link so that more data can be transmitted per second. Many students use Wi-Fi, which is more affected by interference and weak signals than wired connections, so more packets are corrupted and have to be resent, which wastes bandwidth and slows the network. The school could add extra wireless access points to spread the load and use wired Ethernet or fibre for key devices such as servers and teaching computers. It could also limit streaming and large downloads at busy times. Overall the best improvement is to increase bandwidth and add access points, although this costs more money.
worked.q: A school network is very slow at lunchtime when many students use it. Discuss the factors that could be causing this and suggest how the school could improve performance. [6 marks]
steps: Factor 1: number of devices sharing bandwidth.
Factor 3: Wi-Fi as transmission media with interference and errors.
